sections.title: PTH, vitamin D and measuring calcium

blocks.text: **PTH** is an 84-amino-acid peptide made by the parathyroid **chief cells**. A G protein-coupled **calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR)** on these cells detects the **ionised** calcium, and PTH output rises when it falls. PTH then: (1) increases calcium reabsorption and **reduces phosphate reabsorption** in the renal tubule, (2) increases osteoclastic bone resorption, and (3) drives conversion of 25-hydroxyvitamin D to active **1,25(OH)2D**, which boosts gut calcium absorption. A **sustained** PTH excess causes net bone loss, while **pulsatile** PTH builds bone.

blocks.title: Vitamin D pathway (Fig. 24.61)
items: UVB light converts 7-dehydrocholesterol in the skin into vitamin D
The liver adds the 25-hydroxyl group, then the kidney adds the 1α-hydroxyl group to make **1,25(OH)2D**
1,25(OH)2D raises calcium absorption from the diet and increases bone resorption
Failure of renal 1α-hydroxylation is why CKD causes hypocalcaemia, and why native vitamin D does not work in hypoparathyroidism

blocks.title: Measuring calcium
rows: **Total** calcium. Roughly half is bound (mainly to albumin, also citrate and phosphate); the free ionised part is the active one
Add **0.02 mmol/L for every 1 g/L** that albumin is below 40 g/L (subtract if above)
Corrected Ca (mg/dL) = measured Ca + 0.8 × (4 − albumin in g/dL)
Very low albumin (severe acute illness, cirrhosis): measure **ionised calcium** directly
Calcium, phosphate, ALP, renal function, PTH and 25-hydroxyvitamin D

blocks.text: **Low albumin** lowers the total calcium but leaves the ionised calcium normal, so the patient has no symptoms. **Alkalosis** (e.g. hyperventilation) does the opposite: albumin binds more calcium, so the ionised fraction falls while the total stays normal, and the patient can have tetany.

Calcitonin from the thyroid C cells is a tumour marker for medullary thyroid cancer, but it plays **no meaningful role** in normal human calcium balance. Do not list it as a key regulator alongside PTH and vitamin D.

blocks.note: Look at: skin → liver → kidney hydroxylation steps, and where PTH, gut and bone fit in. Useful for explaining vitamin D–driven hypercalcaemia.

blocks.title: Causes of a low calcium
items: **Spurious:** hypoalbuminaemia (ionised calcium normal)
**Low ionised only:** alkalosis, e.g. hyperventilation

**Low PTH:** damage to the glands or their blood supply at thyroid/parathyroid surgery (commonest cause of hypoparathyroidism), autoimmune (APS type 1), DiGeorge syndrome, iron (haemochromatosis) or copper (Wilson's) infiltration, CaSR-activating mutation
**Magnesium depletion:** blocks PTH release and causes PTH resistance; suspect with malabsorption, diuretics, proton pump inhibitors or alcohol excess
**PTH resistance:** pseudohypoparathyroidism
**Low vitamin D:** little UV exposure, malabsorption, enzyme-inducing antiepileptics
**High phosphate:** CKD (failed 1α-hydroxylation plus phosphate retention), phosphate therapy, acute phosphate release (tumour lysis, rhabdomyolysis)
**Calcium sequestration:** acute pancreatitis (calcium binds fatty acids freed by lipase), citrated blood in massive transfusion
**Drugs:** bisphosphonates, calcitonin

blocks.text: "Commonest cause" depends on the book. **Davidson:** a low albumin with normal ionised calcium (spurious). For true hypocalcaemia, **Kumar** names **CKD** and **Step-Up** names **post-thyroidectomy hypoparathyroidism**. Always correct for albumin before calling it hypocalcaemia.

blocks.title: Symptoms and signs
rows: Muscle spasm from overexcitable peripheral nerves. Adults: tingling of hands, feet and around the mouth, plus carpopedal spasm. Children: **triad of carpopedal spasm, stridor (glottic spasm) and convulsions**
Flexed MCP joints with an adducted thumb
Arm cuff pumped above systolic pressure → carpal spasm **within 3 minutes**; the more specific sign of latent tetany
Tapping the facial nerve in front of the ear (over the parotid) makes the facial muscles twitch; less specific
Brisk tendon reflexes, cramps, laryngospasm, seizures
**Long QT** with risk of ventricular arrhythmia; papilloedema when severe
Chronic low Ca with high PO4 (hypoparathyroidism)
Basal ganglia calcification (can cause parkinsonism), epilepsy, psychosis, cataracts
Low Ca with low PO4 (vitamin D lack)
Rickets in children, osteomalacia in adults

blocks.alt: Algorithm: after correcting for albumin, a low or inappropriately normal PTH points to hypoparathyroidism or low magnesium; a high PTH points to CKD, vitamin D deficiency or pseudohypoparathyroidism.

blocks.title: Investigations
items: Albumin-corrected or ionised calcium
Creatinine/eGFR, magnesium, phosphate, ALP, urinary calcium
PTH: absent or inappropriately low in hypoparathyroidism, raised in the other causes
25(OH)D (and 1,25(OH)2D in renal failure or rickets)
Amylase if pancreatitis is possible; ECG for QT
Hand X-ray: **short 4th metacarpals** in pseudohypoparathyroidism

blocks.title: Management
rows: **10–20 mL of 10% calcium gluconate IV over 10–20 min**, then an infusion of about 10 mL/h for several hours if needed, with **cardiac monitoring**
Magnesium chloride 50 mmol IV over 24 h; most is lost in urine so repeat doses may be needed. Calcium is very hard to correct until Mg is replaced
Ergocalciferol or colecalciferol 50 000 IU orally once a week for 8 weeks
Oral calcium plus an **active** vitamin D (alfacalcidol 0.25–2 µg daily or calcitriol), aiming for low-normal calcium
Thiazide diuretic; recombinant PTH (unlicensed, used in hypoparathyroidism but not pseudo) causes less hypercalciuria

blocks.text: **Pseudohypoparathyroidism** is PTH **resistance**: the receptor is normal but a **GNAS1 (Gsα)** signalling defect stops PTH working, so PTH is **high** with low calcium and high phosphate. Type 1a also shows **Albright's hereditary osteodystrophy (AHO)**: short stature, short 4th metacarpals and metatarsals, round face, obesity and subcutaneous calcification. Type 1a appears when the mutation comes from the **mother** (imprinting). Inherited from the **father**, it gives **pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism**: AHO body features with normal calcium and PTH.

Plain colecalciferol **fails in hypoparathyroidism** because PTH is needed for renal 1α-hydroxylation. Use alfacalcidol or calcitriol, and watch for iatrogenic hypercalcaemia, hypercalciuria and nephrocalcinosis.

**Tetany with a normal total calcium** means low ionised calcium from alkalosis: hyperventilation, persistent vomiting, too much antacid, or hypochloraemic alkalosis such as primary hyperaldosteronism. Potassium and magnesium deficiency can also cause tetany.

Step-Up calls pseudohypoparathyroidism autosomal recessive. Follow **Davidson**: it is a GNAS1 defect whose effect depends on which parent passed it on (maternal → PTH resistance; paternal → pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism).

Hypercalcaemia is common and is often found on routine bloods. **Primary hyperparathyroidism and malignancy cause over 90%** of cases. A well **outpatient** usually has primary hyperparathyroidism. In **inpatients**, cancer leads (about 45%), then primary HPT (about 25%) and CKD with tertiary HPT (about 10%). Mild, symptom-free hypercalcaemia affects about 1 in 1000 people, mostly older women.

blocks.title: Causes sorted by PTH (Davidson Box 18.32)
rows: Malignancy: lung, breast, myeloma, renal, lymphoma, thyroid
High 1,25(OH)2D: vitamin D excess, sarcoidosis, TB and other granulomas, HIV, lymphoma
Paget's disease with immobilisation; milk-alkali syndrome; thiazides; vitamin A

blocks.title: Hypercalcaemia of malignancy
items: Seen in up to 20% of cancer patients; about 40% in **myeloma and breast cancer**
**PTHrP** causes about 80% (more bone resorption plus more renal calcium reabsorption); common with squamous, renal, breast and bladder cancers
Bone metastases cause about 20% (local osteolysis, e.g. breast, myeloma); some lymphomas make 1,25(OH)2D; ectopic PTH is rare
New hypercalcaemia in a cancer patient often means progression and should prompt restaging

blocks.title: Symptoms and signs ("stones, bones, groans, psychic moans")
items: **Renal:** polyuria and thirst (calcium blocks urine concentration: a mild **nephrogenic DI**), renal colic, nephrocalcinosis
**GI:** anorexia, nausea, constipation, dyspepsia and peptic ulcer, pancreatitis
**Neuro-psych:** lethargy, depression, drowsiness, poor concentration; **delirium in older people**
**Cardiac:** **short QT**, hypertension
Mild (corrected Ca < 3 mmol/L) is often symptom-free; above 3.8 mmol/L there is dehydration, clouded consciousness and a risk of cardiac arrest
Corneal calcification marks long-standing hypercalcaemia but causes no symptoms

blocks.text: **Hypercalcaemic crisis:** calcium blocks ADH action and lowers GFR, so the patient pees out water, becomes dry, and the calcium climbs further. That vicious cycle is why **IV fluid is always the first step**.

blocks.title: Investigations
items: Repeat and correct the calcium for albumin; check phosphate (low in primary HPT and some cancers), ALP, creatinine
**PTH is the key test.** Detectable or raised PTH with a high calcium = hyperparathyroidism (a 'normal' PTH is inappropriate)
Raised PTH in a young patient or with a family history: 24-h urine calcium or Ca:creatinine clearance ratio to exclude **FHH** (ratio < 0.01)
**PTH suppressed:** look for cancer: CXR, CT, mammogram, protein electrophoresis/immunofixation (myeloma); PTHrP assay if needed (PTH assays do not detect PTHrP)
Also with low PTH: 25(OH)D (high = supplements), 1,25(OH)2D (high = granuloma or lymphoma; then CXR, serum ACE), TSH, short Synacthen test for Addison's

blocks.title: Treating severe hypercalcaemia
rows: Davidson: 2–4 L/day. Kumar: 4–6 L in the first 24 h, then 3–4 L/day. Restores GFR and calcium excretion

With or after rehydration (Davidson: concurrently; Kumar: only after rehydration): **zoledronic acid 4 mg** or **pamidronate 60–90 mg**. Calcium normalises within about 3–5 days; effect lasts up to ~4 weeks; recheck Ca no sooner than 48 h
Works within hours; add for the first 24–48 h in life-threatening cases; loses effect quickly (tachyphylaxis)
Anti-RANKL, 60 mg SC; for malignant hypercalcaemia refractory to zoledronic acid; not renally cleared
Helps in myeloma, sarcoidosis and vitamin D excess; usually useless otherwise
Loop diuretic only if fluid-overloaded; haemodialysis if other measures fail

blocks.text: Saline volumes differ: **Davidson** gives 2–4 L/day, **Kumar** gives 4–6 L over the first 24 h. Follow Davidson for the exam, and remember the volume always depends on the patient's fluid status.
Always review the drug chart: **thiazides** cut renal calcium excretion and **lithium** causes hyperparathyroidism. Giving furosemide to a dry patient worsens the cycle.

blocks.title: Types of hyperparathyroidism
rows: Autonomous gland: single adenoma 90%, multiple adenomas 4%, hyperplasia 5%, carcinoma 1%
All glands enlarge to compensate for low calcium: CKD, vitamin D deficiency, malabsorption
Treat the cause (vitamin D, CKD measures, transplant)
Long-standing secondary HPT turns autonomous, mostly in kidney failure
High (stays high after cause is fixed)
Parathyroidectomy; cinacalcet if surgery fails or is impossible

blocks.text: **Primary HPT** affects about 1 in 800 people, is 2–3 times commoner in women, and 90% of patients are over 50. In **MEN** syndromes all four glands tend to be hyperplastic or carry multiple adenomas.

blocks.title: Clinical picture of primary HPT
items: About **half are asymptomatic**, found on routine bloods; others have fatigue, depression, aches
**Stones:** about 5% of first and 15% of recurrent stone formers have primary HPT; nephrocalcinosis

**Bones:** low BMD on DXA (now the commonest skeletal finding); in advanced disease osteitis fibrosa with **subperiosteal erosions**, terminal phalanx resorption and a **'pepper-pot' skull**; brown tumours and fractures
**Joints:** knee chondrocalcinosis → pseudogout
Hypertension is common; the gland is almost **never palpable**

blocks.title: Diagnosis and localisation
items: High calcium, **low phosphate**, raised or inappropriately normal PTH; often a mild hyperchloraemic acidosis (Cl:PO4 ratio > 33 supports the diagnosis)
Exclude **FHH**: low urinary calcium, Ca:creatinine clearance ratio **< 0.01**, family screening or CaSR gene testing
Only after the biochemistry is clear: localise with **99mTc-sestamibi** (about 90% sensitive) plus neck **ultrasound**
Negative imaging does **not** rule it out; four-gland exploration may be needed

blocks.title: Managing primary HPT
rows: Age < 50, clear symptoms or complications (stones, renal impairment, osteoporosis), or corrected Ca > 2.85 mmol/L (> 11.4 mg/dL)
Ca > 1 mg/dL above the upper limit, CrCl < 60 mL/min, DXA T-score < −2.5
Remove the adenoma; in hyperplasia remove all four glands (Step-Up: with forearm autotransplant)
Older, asymptomatic, mild rise: yearly calcium and renal function, periodic bone density, plenty of fluids
Calcimimetic that sensitises the CaSR and lowers PTH; for patients unfit for or unwilling to have surgery, and for tertiary HPT. May not improve BMD

blocks.text: **After parathyroidectomy** the main danger is **hypocalcaemia from 'hungry bones'**, more likely with marked bone disease or vitamin D deficiency, so correct vitamin D first. Mild transient hypoparathyroidism can last 1–2 weeks; permanent hypoparathyroidism and recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy each occur in < 1% (check the vocal cords before surgery).

**FHH** looks like mild primary HPT, but it is benign and needs no treatment. The real harm is an unnecessary, ineffective parathyroidectomy, so check urinary calcium before referring a young patient or someone with a family history.
Books disagree on how much primary HPT is hyperplasia: **Davidson 5%**, Step-Up < 10%, Pocket Medicine 15–20%. Use Davidson's figures (single adenoma 90%).

blocks.note: Look at: sestamibi scan. At 1 h both thyroid and an enlarged left inferior parathyroid take up tracer; at 3 h only the adenoma still holds it.
Look at: clavicle X-ray with cystic lucent 'brown tumours' of osteitis fibrosa cystica, which predispose to pathological fracture.

blocks.text: Normal plasma phosphate is **0.8–1.4 mmol/L**; hypophosphataemia is below **0.8 mmol/L** (about 2.5 mg/dL), and below **0.4 mmol/L** is severe. About 65% of filtered phosphate is taken back in the **proximal tubule** by sodium–phosphate co-transport. **PTH, FGF23**, volume expansion, osmotic diuretics and glucose infusion all reduce that reabsorption.

blocks.title: Causes by mechanism (Davidson Box 14.22)
rows: **Refeeding** after starvation, respiratory alkalosis, **treatment of DKA**, hungry bone after parathyroidectomy
Malnutrition, alcohol misuse, malabsorption, chronic diarrhoea, phosphate binders and antacids, vitamin D deficiency
Hyperparathyroidism, ECF expansion with diuresis, osmotic diuretics, Fanconi syndrome, familial hypophosphataemic rickets, **tumour-induced osteomalacia** (FGF23)

blocks.text: **Severe** hypophosphataemia is usually seen in **alcohol misuse** and during **DKA treatment**. In **refeeding syndrome**, a carbohydrate load releases insulin, which pushes phosphate, potassium and magnesium into cells and raises ATP demand: arrhythmias, respiratory failure, rhabdomyolysis and fits follow. Prevent it by correcting electrolytes first and raising calories slowly.

blocks.title: Clinical features (low ATP and 2,3-BPG)
items: **Blood:** haemolysis, poor white cell and platelet function; low 2,3-BPG means red cells release less O2
**Muscle:** weakness, rhabdomyolysis; **diaphragm weakness** → respiratory failure and **failure to wean from the ventilator**
**Heart:** reduced contractility, heart failure
**Gut:** ileus
**CNS:** confusion, hallucinations, seizures, coma
**Bone:** osteomalacia if prolonged

blocks.title: Investigations
items: Creatinine, electrolytes, phosphate, albumin, calcium, ALP; in selected cases PTH and 25(OH)D
**Low phosphate + high calcium** → think primary hyperparathyroidism (measure PTH)
**Low phosphate + low calcium** → think hypophosphataemic rickets/osteomalacia
FGF23 excess (X-linked or autosomal dominant hypophosphataemic rickets, tumour-induced osteomalacia): phosphaturia with normal PTH and normal or low 1,25(OH)2D

blocks.title: Management
rows: Oral phosphate (e.g. effervescent tablets, which also carry Na and K) plus high-protein, dairy-rich food; treat the cause
IV sodium or potassium phosphate, e.g. 9–18 mmol in 250–500 mL 5% glucose over 6–12 h
Calcium, phosphate, magnesium and potassium; too-fast infusion can cause severe hypocalcaemia (worse with alkalosis)

blocks.text: **IV phosphate is risky:** it can combine with calcium, causing **hypocalcaemia and metastatic (ectopic) calcification** in kidney and heart. Keep it for critical cases and give it slowly.

blocks.title: Causes of hyperphosphataemia
rows: Hypoparathyroidism, pseudohypoparathyroidism; familial tumoural calcinosis (FGF23 deficiency)
Phosphate enemas or supplements; made worse by inappropriate vitamin D

blocks.title: Clinical features
items: Often silent; problems come from **hypocalcaemia** (tetany, irritability) and **metastatic calcification**
Acute surges (AKI, rhabdomyolysis, tumour lysis) mop up calcium and cause hypocalcaemia
High Ca × PO4 product: uraemic itch, vascular and periarticular calcification; worst in CKD with tertiary HPT
Step-Up (mg/dL units): product > 70 makes calcification likely; CKD goal < 55
Prolonged high phosphate drives hyperparathyroidism

blocks.title: Management by cause
rows: Restrict high-phosphate foods (milk, cheese, eggs, protein-rich foods) + **phosphate binders taken with meals**; aim for phosphate **≤ 1.5 mmol/L** (4.6 mg/dL); dialysis in kidney failure
IV 0.9% saline to increase phosphate excretion

blocks.text: **Binders:** calcium carbonate/acetate, aluminium hydroxide, lanthanum carbonate and sevelamer. **Sevelamer** (unlike calcium binders) slows vascular calcification and lowers cholesterol. **Aluminium** works well but risks aluminium bone disease and cognitive impairment. Adherence is poor, and overly strict diets cause protein malnutrition.

**Renal bone disease (CKD–MBD):** the failing kidney retains phosphate and cannot make 1,25(OH)2D. High phosphate raises **FGF23** and PTH; low 1,25(OH)2D cuts calcium absorption, and calcium phosphate deposits in tissues, so calcium falls and PTH climbs further (**secondary HPT**). The results are **osteitis fibrosa cystica**, calcification of vessels and heart valves, and sometimes **tertiary HPT** with hypercalcaemia. Too much vitamin D causes **adynamic bone disease**.

blocks.title: CKD–MBD: labs and X-ray signs
items: Secondary HPT labs: **low Ca, high PO4, high PTH, high ALP**
X-ray: digital subperiosteal erosions, 'pepperpot' skull
**'Rugger jersey' spine**: alternating sclerotic and porotic bands from long-standing HPT
Adynamic bone: low PTH, normal ALP, may be hypercalcaemic

blocks.title: Treating renal bone disease (Davidson)
rows: Alfacalcidol or calcitriol if hypocalcaemic or PTH > 2× upper limit; titrate PTH to **2–4× upper limit**; avoid hypercalcaemia
Persistent hypercalcaemia → parathyroidectomy; **cinacalcet** if surgery fails or is not possible

blocks.text: PTH thresholds vary: **Davidson** starts active vitamin D at PTH > 2× the upper limit and aims for 2–4×; **Kumar** starts at ≥ 3×. Over-suppressing PTH risks adynamic bone. Use Davidson's numbers.

**Calciphylaxis** (calcific uraemic arteriolopathy): painful skin plaques and ulcers with non-healing eschars in CKD. Risk factors: hyperparathyroidism, high phosphate, morbid obesity and **warfarin**. Histology shows calcified skin microvessels without vasculitis.

blocks.note: Look at: flow chart of renal osteodystrophy: low 1,25(OH)2D and high phosphate → low calcium → parathyroid hyperplasia → osteoclastic resorption.
Look at: CKD–MBD summary of mechanisms with X-ray signs (subperiosteal erosions, pepperpot skull, rugger jersey spine).

cards.front: How do you correct total calcium for a low albumin (SI units)?
cards.back: Add 0.02 mmol/L for every 1 g/L that albumin is below 40 g/L. If albumin is very low, measure ionised calcium instead.

cards.front: What does alkalosis do to total and ionised calcium?
cards.back: Total calcium stays normal, but more calcium binds albumin so ionised calcium falls; tetany can occur.
Inflate an arm cuff above systolic pressure; carpal spasm within 3 minutes indicates latent tetany. It is more specific than Chvostek's sign.

cards.front: Hypoparathyroidism vs pseudohypoparathyroidism vs vitamin D deficiency: phosphate and PTH?
cards.back: Hypopara: PO4 high, PTH low. Pseudohypopara: PO4 high, PTH high. Vitamin D deficiency: PO4 low, PTH high.
10–20 mL of 10% calcium gluconate IV over 10–20 min, then an infusion (~10 mL/h) if needed, with cardiac monitoring.

cards.front: Why does magnesium depletion cause hypocalcaemia?
cards.back: It impairs PTH secretion (PTH low or inappropriately normal) and causes end-organ PTH resistance. Replace magnesium first.

cards.front: Which two causes account for over 90% of hypercalcaemia?
Commonest mechanism of hypercalcaemia of malignancy?
cards.back: PTHrP secretion (~80%); bone metastases cause ~20%. PTH itself is suppressed.

cards.front: First two steps in severe hypercalcaemia (Davidson Box 33.13)?
cards.back: IV 0.9% saline (2–4 L/day), then an IV bisphosphonate: zoledronic acid 4 mg or pamidronate 60–90 mg.

cards.front: What urine test separates FHH from primary hyperparathyroidism?
cards.back: Urinary calcium: Ca:creatinine clearance ratio < 0.01 (low urinary calcium) in FHH.

cards.front: Davidson indications for surgery in primary hyperparathyroidism?
cards.back: Age < 50, clear symptoms or complications (stones, renal impairment, osteoporosis), or corrected Ca > 2.85 mmol/L.
Secondary: calcium low or low-normal (compensatory). Tertiary: calcium high, with PTH still high after the cause is corrected.

cards.front: Two classic settings for severe hypophosphataemia?
cards.back: Alcohol misuse/refeeding and treatment of diabetic ketoacidosis.

cards.front: Main risk of IV phosphate replacement?
cards.back: Calcium phosphate precipitation: hypocalcaemia and metastatic calcification. Reserve for severe cases (< 0.4 mmol/L, symptomatic).
≤ 1.5 mmol/L (4.6 mg/dL), using diet plus phosphate binders taken with meals.
Alternating sclerotic and porotic vertebral bands on X-ray from long-standing hyperparathyroidism in CKD.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man with alcohol-related liver disease has a total serum calcium of 1.95 mmol/L on routine bloods. His serum albumin is 25 g/L. He has no tingling or cramps.
questions.leadIn: What is his albumin-adjusted calcium?
questions.explanation: Albumin is 15 g/L below 40, so add 15 × 0.02 = 0.30 mmol/L: 1.95 + 0.30 = **2.25 mmol/L**, which is normal and fits his lack of symptoms. With albumin this low in cirrhosis the correction is less reliable, so an ionised calcium is the better test.
whyNot: This subtracts the correction instead of adding it.
This ignores the low albumin.
This adds only half the correction (0.01 per g/L).
This adds double the correction.

questions.stem: A 23-year-old woman is brought in after a panic attack. She is breathing fast, has tingling around the lips and her hands are in spasm. Total calcium is 2.38 mmol/L and albumin 42 g/L.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely mechanism of her symptoms?
options: Fall in ionised calcium from alkalosis
questions.explanation: Hyperventilation causes a respiratory alkalosis. More calcium binds albumin, so the **ionised** fraction falls and tetany occurs while the total calcium is normal.
whyNot: Her albumin is normal, and low albumin lowers total calcium without symptoms.
There is no malabsorption, diuretic, PPI or alcohol history, and total calcium is normal.
Hypoparathyroidism lowers total calcium, which is normal here.
Vitamin D deficiency gives a low total calcium and low phosphate, not acute symptoms with normal calcium.

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the most likely cause of the low calcium. Any option can be picked for several items, or for none.

items.stem: A 46-year-old woman has tingling fingers and lips 2 days after a total thyroidectomy for Graves' disease. Trousseau's sign is positive. Corrected calcium 1.74 mmol/L, phosphate 1.9 mmol/L, PTH undetectable.
items.explanation: Low calcium, high phosphate and an absent PTH straight after thyroid surgery: the glands or their blood supply were damaged. This is the commonest cause of hypoparathyroidism.

items.stem: A 15-year-old boy has a first seizure. He is short with a round face, and his 4th knuckles are missing when he makes a fist. Corrected calcium 1.82 mmol/L, phosphate high, PTH several times the upper limit, 25(OH)D normal, creatinine normal.
items.explanation: High PTH but still low calcium and high phosphate means the body is not responding to PTH. Short 4th metacarpals, short stature and round face are Albright's hereditary osteodystrophy: pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1a.

items.stem: A 57-year-old man who drinks heavily and takes omeprazole has chronic diarrhoea. Corrected calcium 1.85 mmol/L, PTH low-normal, phosphate normal. IV calcium gluconate raises the calcium only briefly. Serum magnesium is 0.32 mmol/L.
items.explanation: Low magnesium stops PTH release (inappropriately low PTH) and causes PTH resistance. Alcohol, PPIs and diarrhoea all deplete magnesium, and calcium will not stay up until magnesium is replaced.

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the most likely cause of the raised calcium. Any option can be picked for several items, or for none.

items.stem: A 67-year-old smoker has 2 months of weight loss and blood-streaked sputum, and is now drowsy. Corrected calcium 3.6 mmol/L, PTH undetectable. CXR shows a right hilar mass; there are no lytic bone lesions.
items.explanation: Suppressed PTH with a lung mass and no bone lesions points to humoral hypercalcaemia from PTHrP, the mechanism in about 80% of malignant hypercalcaemia (common with squamous tumours).

items.stem: A 36-year-old woman has a dry cough and red eyes. CXR shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. Corrected calcium 2.92 mmol/L, PTH suppressed, 25(OH)D normal, 1,25(OH)2D raised.
items.explanation: High 1,25(OH)2D with normal 25(OH)D means unregulated 1α-hydroxylation by granulomas. Hilar nodes, cough and eye inflammation fit sarcoidosis.

items.stem: A 73-year-old man has back pain, tiredness and recurrent chest infections. Hb 92 g/L, creatinine 190 µmol/L, corrected calcium 3.1 mmol/L, PTH low, ALP normal.
items.explanation: Two steps: low PTH means a non-parathyroid cause; bone pain with anaemia, infections and renal impairment suggests myeloma, which needs protein electrophoresis. Myeloma is one of the cancers most often linked to hypercalcaemia.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman has a corrected calcium of 2.78 mmol/L on a health check. Phosphate is 0.7 mmol/L, PTH is at the top of the reference range, and 24-hour urinary calcium is high. eGFR is normal.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A PTH in the normal range while calcium is high is **inappropriate**: PTH should be suppressed. Low phosphate and high urinary calcium (excluding FHH) confirm primary hyperparathyroidism.
whyNot: FHH has low urinary calcium (Ca:creatinine clearance ratio < 0.01).
Secondary HPT has a low or low-normal calcium.
Tertiary HPT follows long-standing secondary HPT, usually in kidney failure; her eGFR is normal.
Malignancy suppresses PTH.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old man has a corrected calcium of 2.67 mmol/L and a PTH slightly above the reference range. He feels well. His father was told he had 'high calcium' years ago and never needed treatment. Urinary Ca:creatinine clearance ratio is 0.005.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate management?
options: Sestamibi scan to localise an adenoma
questions.explanation: The very low urinary calcium ratio (< 0.01) and family history point to **familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia**. It is benign and needs no treatment; family screening or CaSR gene testing confirms it.
whyNot: Parathyroidectomy does not work in FHH, and an unneeded operation is the main risk of misdiagnosis.
There is no indication to lower calcium in benign FHH.
Localisation is only done after primary HPT is confirmed biochemically.
Bisphosphonates are for severe symptomatic hypercalcaemia.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman with anorexia nervosa (BMI 13) is started on high-calorie nasogastric feeding. On day 3 she becomes weak and confused and has runs of ectopic beats.
questions.leadIn: Which electrolyte abnormality is most likely?
questions.explanation: This is **refeeding syndrome**: carbohydrate triggers insulin, which drives phosphate (with potassium and magnesium) into cells. Low phosphate causes weakness, confusion and arrhythmias. Prevent it by correcting electrolytes first and raising calories slowly.
whyNot: Insulin drives potassium into cells, so potassium falls.
Refeeding does not raise calcium.
Sodium is not the key disturbance in refeeding.
Magnesium falls, not rises, in refeeding.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old man in intensive care was treated for diabetic ketoacidosis 4 days ago. He keeps failing ventilator weaning trials. Serum phosphate is 0.3 mmol/L; calcium and potassium are normal.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate treatment?
options: IV phosphate 18 mmol as a 10-minute bolus
No treatment; recheck in a week
questions.explanation: Phosphate below 0.4 mmol/L with diaphragm weakness is severe and symptomatic, so IV phosphate is justified. It is given **slowly** with checks of calcium, phosphate, magnesium and potassium.
whyNot: Fast infusion can precipitate calcium phosphate and cause severe hypocalcaemia and ectopic calcification.
Binders lower phosphate further.
Calcium does not treat low phosphate and adds precipitation risk.
Severe symptomatic hypophosphataemia needs replacement now.

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the most likely cause of the raised phosphate. Any option can be picked for several items, or for none.

items.stem: A 59-year-old man with a bulky high-grade lymphoma starts chemotherapy. Two days later potassium, urate and phosphate are high, calcium is low and creatinine is rising.
items.explanation: Cells broken down by chemotherapy release potassium, phosphate and nucleic acids (urate). The phosphate surge binds calcium, causing hypocalcaemia.

items.stem: An 81-year-old woman is found on her kitchen floor after lying there for 2 days. Her urine is dark brown; CK is 48 000 U/L, phosphate high, calcium low.
items.explanation: Prolonged lying leads to muscle breakdown, which releases phosphate from damaged cells; a very high CK and dark urine confirm rhabdomyolysis.

items.stem: A 52-year-old man has been on haemodialysis for 9 years and complains of itch. Calcium and phosphate are both high and PTH is 15 times the upper limit. Alfacalcidol was stopped 3 months ago but the calcium has not fallen.
items.explanation: Two steps: years of secondary HPT in kidney failure, then hypercalcaemia that persists off vitamin D. The glands have become autonomous: tertiary hyperparathyroidism with a high Ca × PO4 product causing itch.

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the diagnosis that best fits the results. Any option can be picked for several items, or for none.
options: Secondary hyperparathyroidism from vitamin D deficiency

items.stem: A 74-year-old housebound woman has proximal weakness and aching bones. Corrected calcium 2.06 mmol/L, phosphate 0.65 mmol/L, ALP raised, PTH high, 25(OH)D very low, creatinine normal.
items.explanation: Low calcium and low phosphate with a high PTH and very low 25(OH)D: the parathyroids are compensating for vitamin D lack (osteomalacia).

items.stem: A 20-year-old man is short and has short 4th metacarpals and subcutaneous calcified nodules. Calcium and PTH are normal. His father has the same hand appearance.
items.explanation: AHO features with normal calcium and PTH, passed from the father, is pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism (GNAS1 mutation on the paternal chromosome).

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman had a successful kidney transplant 1 year ago; creatinine is now normal. Corrected calcium 2.84 mmol/L, PTH still high, phosphate low-normal.
items.explanation: Two steps: the original drive (kidney failure) has been removed, yet PTH stays high and calcium is now raised. Long-standing secondary HPT has become autonomous: tertiary HPT.

items.stem: A 66-year-old man is septic on the ward. Total calcium 1.92 mmol/L, albumin 21 g/L, ionised calcium normal, PTH normal. He has no tetany.
items.explanation: Normal ionised calcium and normal PTH: the low total is due to low albumin (the commonest cause of a low total calcium per Davidson).

questions.stem: A 62-year-old woman with a corrected calcium of 3.3 mmol/L has an ECG before admission.
questions.leadIn: Which ECG change is expected from the hypercalcaemia?
questions.explanation: High calcium **shortens** the QT; low calcium prolongs it.
whyNot: A long QT is the hypocalcaemia pattern.
Peaked T waves suggest hyperkalaemia.
U waves suggest hypokalaemia.
Delta waves mark ventricular pre-excitation.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with hypercalcaemia (corrected calcium 3.0 mmol/L) passes 4 L of dilute urine a day despite feeling thirsty. Glucose is normal.
questions.leadIn: What best explains his polyuria?
questions.explanation: Calcium reduces the tubules' ability to concentrate urine and blocks ADH action, giving a mild **nephrogenic DI**. The water loss raises calcium further.
whyNot: Glucose is normal.
ADH production is not the problem; the kidney fails to respond.
Thirst here is the result of the polyuria, not its cause.
He is not on a diuretic.

questions.stem: A 49-year-old woman is listed for removal of a parathyroid adenoma. She has bone pain with subperiosteal erosions on hand X-ray, and her 25(OH)D is low.
questions.leadIn: Which pre-operative step best lowers her risk of post-operative hypocalcaemia?
questions.explanation: Marked bone disease and vitamin D deficiency predict **hungry bone** hypocalcaemia after parathyroidectomy. Correcting vitamin D beforehand reduces that risk.
whyNot: A bisphosphonate does not prevent hungry bone and could lower calcium further.
Thiazides raise calcium and are not used for this.
Cinacalcet is for patients not having surgery.
Restricting calcium would worsen post-operative hypocalcaemia.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man on dialysis has had poorly controlled phosphate for years. He has taken the same binder for a long time and now has worsening memory and bone pain.
questions.leadIn: Which binder is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation: Absorbed **aluminium** causes aluminium bone disease and cognitive impairment, which is why aluminium binders are now rarely used long term.
whyNot: Sevelamer is a non-absorbed polymer; its known extras are less vascular calcification and lower cholesterol.
Calcium binders add a calcium load (vascular calcification) but do not cause cognitive decline.
Lanthanum carbonate is a non-aluminium binder; it is not the cause of aluminium bone disease and cognitive impairment.
As for calcium carbonate: calcium load, not cognitive impairment.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old woman with known metastatic breast cancer is brought in confused and vomiting. She has dry mucous membranes and a postural drop. Corrected calcium is 3.8 mmol/L, creatinine is raised.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate first step?
options: IV zoledronic acid before any fluid
questions.explanation: **Step 1:** recognise severe hypercalcaemia (> 3.5 mmol/L) as an emergency whatever the cause. **Step 2:** note she is dry: calcium has caused polyuria and a fall in GFR, which drives calcium higher. **Step 3:** break the cycle with IV 0.9% saline (Davidson 2–4 L/day), which restores GFR and calcium excretion. **Step 4:** once rehydrated, give an IV bisphosphonate (zoledronic acid 4 mg or pamidronate 60–90 mg); calcitonin can bridge the first 24–48 h, and denosumab is kept for cases refractory to zoledronic acid.
whyNot: Bisphosphonates are given alongside or after rehydration; alone they act too slowly and are harder on dry kidneys.
Loop diuretics are only for fluid-overloaded patients and worsen dehydration.
Steroids help mainly in myeloma, sarcoidosis and vitamin D excess.
Denosumab is for hypercalcaemia refractory to zoledronic acid.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman who rarely goes outside has aching bones and difficulty rising from a chair. Corrected calcium 2.02 mmol/L, phosphate 0.62 mmol/L, ALP raised, PTH high, creatinine normal, magnesium normal.
questions.leadIn: Which test will best confirm the cause?
questions.explanation: **Step 1:** albumin-corrected calcium is truly low. **Step 2:** PTH is high, so the parathyroids work and are responding. **Step 3:** with high PTH, phosphate separates the causes: high in CKD or pseudohypoparathyroidism, **low in vitamin D deficiency**. Creatinine is normal. **Step 4:** housebound, proximal myopathy and raised ALP fit osteomalacia, so measure 25(OH)D.
whyNot: Antibodies are for idiopathic hypoparathyroidism, where PTH is low.
Sestamibi localises adenomas in primary HPT, which raises calcium.
Amylase is for pancreatitis, which presents acutely with abdominal pain.
Synacthen tests for Addison's, a cause of high calcium.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman with fatigue and a past kidney stone has a phosphate of 0.65 mmol/L. Corrected calcium is 2.81 mmol/L, creatinine and albumin are normal.
questions.leadIn: What is the most useful next test?
questions.explanation: **Step 1:** low phosphate is the starting abnormality. **Step 2:** look at calcium: **low phosphate with high calcium** suggests primary hyperparathyroidism (PTH blocks proximal phosphate reabsorption and raises calcium). **Step 3:** a stone history fits. **Step 4:** measure PTH; a raised or inappropriately normal value confirms it.
whyNot: FGF23 excess lowers phosphate but calcium is normal or low.
25(OH)D lack gives low calcium, not high.
Amylase has no role here.
Bone biopsy is invasive and not a diagnostic step for this picture.

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the most appropriate next treatment. Any option can be picked for several items, or for none.

items.stem: A 33-year-old woman has carpopedal spasm and noisy breathing on the second day after a total thyroidectomy. Corrected calcium 1.58 mmol/L; the ECG shows a long QT.
items.explanation: Severe symptomatic hypocalcaemia with stridor and a long QT needs IV calcium gluconate (10–20 mL of 10% over 10–20 min) under cardiac monitoring.

items.stem: A 76-year-old man with lung cancer and hypercalcaemia has had IV fluids and two doses of zoledronic acid. A week later his corrected calcium is still 3.4 mmol/L.
items.explanation: Malignant hypercalcaemia refractory to zoledronic acid: Davidson lists SC denosumab (anti-RANKL) as the alternative.

items.stem: A 59-year-old man has primary hyperparathyroidism with a corrected calcium of 2.95 mmol/L. He has severe COPD, the anaesthetist judges him unfit for surgery, and he does not want an operation.
items.explanation: Cinacalcet makes the CaSR more sensitive and lowers PTH; it is licensed for primary HPT in patients unfit for or unwilling to have surgery.

items.stem: A 44-year-old woman with sarcoidosis has a corrected calcium of 3.1 mmol/L despite rehydration. PTH is suppressed and 1,25(OH)2D is high.
items.explanation: Glucocorticoids (prednisolone 30–60 mg/day) work in calcitriol-driven hypercalcaemia such as sarcoidosis, myeloma and vitamin D excess.

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the most likely cause of the low phosphate. Any option can be picked for several items, or for none.

items.stem: A 19-year-old with type 1 diabetes was admitted with pH 7.05 and ketones 6 mmol/L. After 36 hours of insulin infusion and fluids he feels weak; phosphate is 0.32 mmol/L.
items.explanation: Insulin given to treat DKA drives phosphate into cells, one of the classic causes of severe hypophosphataemia.

items.stem: A 47-year-old woman had a large parathyroid adenoma removed yesterday; she had marked bone disease. Corrected calcium 1.80 mmol/L, phosphate 0.4 mmol/L, magnesium low.
items.explanation: After PTH falls suddenly, demineralised bone takes up calcium, phosphate and magnesium: hungry bone syndrome.

items.stem: A 54-year-old man has 2 years of bone pain, proximal weakness and several fractures. Phosphate is low with phosphaturia; calcium and PTH normal; 1,25(OH)2D low. MRI finds a small soft-tissue tumour in his thigh.
items.explanation: Two steps: renal phosphate wasting with normal PTH and low 1,25(OH)2D means FGF23 excess; new onset in an adult with a tumour means tumour-induced osteomalacia.

items.stem: A 71-year-old man with chronic dyspepsia has been taking large amounts of an aluminium-containing antacid for months. Phosphate is low; calcium, PTH and renal function are normal.
items.explanation: Aluminium antacids bind dietary phosphate in the gut and block its absorption.

questions.stem: A junior doctor wants to check for latent tetany in a patient with a borderline low calcium.
questions.leadIn: Which bedside sign is the more specific test?
questions.explanation: Inflating an arm cuff above systolic pressure for up to 3 minutes causes carpal spasm in latent tetany (Trousseau's). Chvostek's facial twitch is less specific.
whyNot: Chvostek's sign is less specific for hypocalcaemia.
Babinski's sign tests the corticospinal tract.
Hoffmann's sign tests for an upper motor neurone lesion.
Tinel's sign tests for nerve entrapment.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old woman has had untreated primary hyperparathyroidism for many years and now has hand pain. A hand X-ray is taken.
questions.leadIn: Which finding is most characteristic?
questions.explanation: Advanced primary HPT causes subperiosteal resorption (classically on the radial side of the 2nd and 3rd fingers) and terminal tuft resorption, plus a 'pepper-pot' skull.
whyNot: Looser's zones are pseudofractures of osteomalacia.
Pencil-in-cup is psoriatic arthritis.
Marginal erosions with periarticular osteopenia suggest rheumatoid arthritis.
Rugger jersey spine is a spinal (not hand) sign of renal bone disease.

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single most useful next investigation. Any option can be picked for several items, or for none.

items.stem: A 28-year-old woman has a corrected calcium of 2.69 mmol/L on routine testing and a mildly raised PTH. Her mother has had a 'slightly high calcium' for years without treatment.
items.explanation: Young age and family history: exclude FHH with urinary calcium (Ca:creatinine clearance ratio < 0.01 in FHH) before anyone considers surgery.

items.stem: A 62-year-old woman with a corrected calcium of 2.96 mmol/L, raised PTH and high-normal urinary calcium has a kidney stone and is booked for parathyroidectomy.
items.explanation: The diagnosis is already made biochemically. Imaging now localises the adenoma so the surgeon can do a targeted resection.

items.stem: A 51-year-old man has a corrected calcium of 2.80 mmol/L with an undetectable PTH. He has lost weight, has darker skin and feels faint on standing. Sodium 128 mmol/L, potassium 5.6 mmol/L.
items.explanation: Two steps: suppressed PTH means a non-parathyroid cause; pigmentation, postural hypotension, low sodium and high potassium point to adrenal failure, a cause of hypercalcaemia, so do a short Synacthen test.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man with squamous cell lung cancer has a corrected calcium of 3.4 mmol/L. PTH is suppressed and a bone scan shows no metastases.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely mechanism of his hypercalcaemia?
questions.explanation: PTHrP causes about 80% of malignant hypercalcaemia: it acts on the PTH receptor to increase bone resorption and renal calcium reabsorption, but is not detected by PTH assays.
whyNot: The bone scan shows no metastases.
Ectopic PTH is rare and PTH is suppressed here.
Calcitriol production is a feature of some lymphomas.
Immobilisation causes hypercalcaemia mainly with high bone turnover such as Paget's.

questions.stem: A 57-year-old woman on haemodialysis with poorly controlled phosphate and hyperparathyroidism takes warfarin for atrial fibrillation. She has very painful, hard plaques on her thighs that have ulcerated and formed non-healing eschars. Skin biopsy shows calcified small vessels without vasculitis.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Calcific uraemic arteriolopathy: painful plaques and necrotic ulcers in CKD. Risk factors include hyperparathyroidism, high phosphate, obesity and warfarin. Biopsy shows calcified microvessels without vasculitis.
whyNot: Pyoderma gangrenosum starts as a painful nodule or pustule that ulcerates with an undermined edge, usually with IBD or inflammatory arthritis; its histology is non-specific, not calcified vessels.
The biopsy specifically shows no vasculitis.
Necrotising fasciitis is an infection spreading fast along the fascial plane, with pain out of proportion to the skin signs; it does not calcify vessels.
Cholesterol emboli follow arterial surgery or angiography in widespread atheroma and cause livedo and ischaemic toes with renal impairment, not calcified skin microvessels.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old man with CKD stage 4 has corrected calcium 2.08 mmol/L, phosphate 1.8 mmol/L and PTH 5 times the upper limit; 25(OH)D is replete. He already follows a low-phosphate diet and takes a binder with meals.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate next step?
questions.explanation: Davidson: give active vitamin D (alfacalcidol or calcitriol) when the patient is hypocalcaemic or PTH is more than twice the upper limit, aiming for PTH 2–4× the upper limit without causing hypercalcaemia.
whyNot: Parathyroidectomy is for tertiary HPT with persistent hypercalcaemia; his calcium is low.
Cinacalcet is used when parathyroidectomy fails or is not possible in tertiary HPT.
Bisphosphonates lower calcium, which is already low.
Furosemide does not treat secondary hyperparathyroidism.

ospe.identify: 99mTc-sestamibi scan: tracer in thyroid and an enlarged left inferior parathyroid at 1 h, but only the parathyroid at 3 h → **parathyroid adenoma** (primary hyperparathyroidism).
Clavicle X-ray with lytic cystic lesions → **brown tumours of osteitis fibrosa cystica** (severe hyperparathyroidism); risk of pathological fracture.
CKD–mineral bone disorder radiology: **subperiosteal erosions**, **pepperpot skull**, **rugger jersey spine** (secondary/tertiary HPT) vs Looser's zones (osteomalacia).
Skin biopsy with calcified small arteries and no vasculitis → **calciphylaxis** (calcific uraemic arteriolopathy) in CKD.
